title: How Molly Meldrum changed Australian Music
transcript:
Speaker 1: Welcome to Countdown from Perth. And now it's over to Molly. Molly!
Speaker 2: For a generation of Australians, Molly Meldrum's Countdown was the soundtrack of their youth. Credited with engineering the breakthroughs of acts like ABBA, Blondie and Madonna in Australia, he was as loved by the world's biggest music stars as he was by Australian music fans. A kingmaker of Australian music, the man dubbed The Guru passed peacefully in hospital at the age of 83.
Speaker 3: As Kai sums it up with one song, and I think this applies to me, I shall be so lucky, and I've been very lucky.
Speaker 2: I'm Ruby Jones, and you're listening to 7am. Today, music journalist and friend of Molly Meldrum, Jane Gazzo, on his incredible legacy. It's Monday, November 23.
Speaker 1: Jane, hello. Welcome to the show. Thank you so much for coming on. Oh, you're welcome.
Speaker 2: So Jane, I know that Molly was a friend and a mentor to you and I'm really sorry for your loss. Maybe we can begin by talking a bit about who Molly was to you privately. He had this enormous public personality as a music journalist, as a producer, and of course, as a TV host.
Speaker 1: But tell me a bit more about the Molly that you knew. I liken him to a favourite uncle because I grew up watching Molly Meldrum on Countdown, as did many Australians throughout the 70s and 80s and 90s on Hey Hey. So for me, he was part of the furniture. He was an uncle, like a favourite uncle, that came into my lounge room every Sunday night on Countdown, presenting the best bands, the greatest music, and making the art of interviewing pop stars look like the most glamorous job in the world. And as a youngster growing up in the northern suburbs of Melbourne, that appealed to me. I loved that.
Speaker 3: Now from the Australian end, on our 100th Countdown, we've got Supernaught, LRB, Daryl Braithwaite, Renee Geyer, John Paul Young.
Speaker 1: There was a warmth about Molly that he could just get the best out of his interviewees. There you go, that was my sense. My zest or my sex? My sex. My sex.
Speaker 3: Yes.
Speaker 1: The band's called My Sex as well? From New Zealand.
Speaker 3: Yeah.
Speaker 1: Which sex is it? I don't know. You don't know? You of all people don't know? It's a sex that you've never experienced before? I find this very hard to believe. Your reputation precedes you, Mr Melvin. He was someone I really looked up to, but also he represented what I wanted to do and be when I grew up. So when I got the chance, I became a radio announcer. I started out in community radio and then got onto Triple J, which led to hosting Recovery, which was the successor to Countdown on the ABC after Countdown finished in 87. There were a few music shows like Countdown Revolution, etc., that the ABC kind of toyed with. But it was around about 95, 96 that they brought Recovery onto the ABC. And I got the job of co-host. And Recovery was filmed at the Countdown Studios, the old Countdown Studios in Ripon Lee.
Speaker 3: So.
Speaker 1: Molly's dressing room was still there and on Quiet Moments on Recovery, which was a live television show, I would go and sit in Molly's old dressing room just hoping that the energy of Molly would seep off the walls onto me, which I know sounds really silly, but I was so invested in Not becoming the next Molly Meldrum, but wanting to be as good as Molly.
Speaker 2: Yeah, maybe we can talk a little bit more about Molly as the host of Countdown. So that was his big break and that was Australia's kind of first big music TV show.
Speaker 1: What is Countdown?
Speaker 3: Well, Countdown is the most exciting visual presentation of the top 40 hits you'll ever see on colour television.
Speaker 2: Of course, we all know him as the host of Countdown, but he was actually never really supposed to be the host.
Speaker 1: He was originally hired as.
Speaker 2: the talent booker, but then he became the talent.
Speaker 1: That's right. That's right. Molly was only supposed to be the talent booker. He had, of course, carved a career in music journalism with the brilliant music magazine Ghost Sets. But yes, originally, Countdown, I think, was only ever meant to run on the ABC for eight weeks or something like that. They had a radio host from Brisbane that was going to be the host. And of course, as all great stories, one time that host didn't show up on set. and Molly was thrust in.
Speaker 3: As talent coordinator of Countdown, I must say that I'm absolutely amazed at the amount of work, time and pre-planning that is involved in putting together such a show. All of us on the Countdown production team are convinced that this will be the best pop show ever produced on Australian television.
Speaker 1: And it was because of his... I guess, warm nature and kind of incoherent mumbling, perhaps, that he quickly became the host and he found his feet. I mean, there was something like 563 episodes of Countdown. So, you know, he fit that role so beautifully. He was well-researched. As I said, he had that warmth and that rapport with artists. So, you know, it was a happy mistake.
Speaker 3: We've been searching around what better group to start off with in London than our own Australian.
Speaker 1: Group, and it's ACDC.
Speaker 3: Fancy meeting you here, mate.
Speaker 1: Yeah, isn't it marvelous?
Speaker 2: Yeah, you could tell that those artists, a lot of them really loved him, right? And they loved being interviewed him. People like Madonna, you can tell in that interview that she's enjoying herself.
Speaker 1: Hi, I'm Madonna.
Speaker 2: And I want to wish everybody in Australia Merry Christmas.
Speaker 1: Just say it properly, please. That is proper.
Speaker 3: It's not f * * * ing proper.
Speaker 1: Hi, I'm Madonna and I want to wish everybody in Australia Merry Christmas.
Speaker 3: Oh, it sounds so sincere.
Speaker 1: I mean, I don't know, we can't wait. Oh, look, he had a rapport with all of us. I mean, you speak to anyone that was on the show or came into Molly's line of fire, you know, during the 70s and 80s, during Countdown, and they'll all tell you. There was a real fond affection for him, and he earned that. You know, that was just the charm of Molly.
Speaker 3: What's wrong with you?
Speaker 1: Don't you see? You behave yourself. Now, listen, we've got to ask you some sensible questions.
Speaker 3: The first time was a couple of years ago. Hi.
Speaker 2: Was with Iggy.
Speaker 3: Will you concentrate on the questions?
Speaker 2: And, I mean, some of his interviews kind of are famous for going.
Speaker 1: Off the rails as well, right? His interview with Prince Charles, for example. Do you remember watching that? I think Prince Charles said, I wasn't quite prepared for Molly Meldrum. I don't think any interviewer is.
Speaker 3: The profits from which will be donated to the Queen's Silver Jubilee organisation.
Speaker 1: Oh, f * * *. They didn't have the autocue. They didn't have that in those days, late 70s, when Molly was interviewing Prince Charles and Molly was trying to get the intro to a Prince's Trust gig right and he couldn't because there was no autocue and teleprompter and he was very nervous. I mean, he's got Prince Charles, who would be the future King of England, next to him.
Speaker 3: The poor guy, um....
Speaker 1: Yeah molly did say at the time you know if if anything could have swallowed him up he wished then and there to be swallowed up but um he's worn it as a badge of pride i think since and that kind of style his style um you know he wasn't the most articulate speaker but he was natural and and you know that really endeared him to the audience even more that kind of lack of polish and he had this ability to laugh at himself as well. We saw that throughout his career, particularly on Hey Hey Saturday.
Speaker 2: That was a big part of why people loved to watch him.
Speaker 3: You saw last week on Hey Hey, I nearly said Bloody Countdown.
Speaker 1: You saw last week on Hey Hey. Someone said to me that Molly was a great TV presenter because he wasn't a great TV presenter. So he wasn't polished. He was a little bit amateur in a sense, but that's what worked for Countdown and that put people at ease so quickly. So, again, the ability to, I guess, exude this warmth and everybody's mate really, really worked for Molly.
Speaker 2: Coming up, how Molly Meldrum shaped the trajectory of the Australian music industry. Let's talk about his influence on the music industry. Elton John once described Molly as the single most important influence on Australian pop music.
Speaker 1: So... Just how influential was.
Speaker 2: Countdown and Molly Meldrum on the... trajectory of the Australian music industry.
Speaker 1: Well, incredibly, incredibly. I'd say he's responsible for most of the household names that we know and love now from the 70s and 80s were due in part to him having them on Countdown. I mean, if you got on Countdown in the 70s and 80s, there's probably an 85, 90% chance that you would become a household name. You know, if Molly championed you, you were, you know, you were well on your way and, you know, Skyhooks, John Farnham, Sherbert, ACDC, Daryl Braithwaite, Madonna, Blondie, the Ramones, Elton John, ABBA, Rod Stewart. I mean, those were all artists that we first saw on Countdown. In fact, Molly famously played the incorrect single of Blondie's. He played Sunday Girl instead of whatever song that they had released overseas. And that became a hit here in Australia because Molly had played it on Countdown and suddenly they have an audience here, for example.
Speaker 3: When I'm trying to sort of say is um blondie i mean deborah um i'm sorry oh just could you write just a second just a minute as you can see this interview is getting absolutely.
Speaker 1: Nowhere Peter Andre just did a really touching tribute today. I mean, Peter Andre appeared on New Faces where Molly was a judge. Now, I don't think Peter Andre won that heat of New Faces, but Molly saw something in him that the other judges didn't. And lo and behold, takes him under his wing. And Peter Andre has three number one hits in the UK in the 90s, owes his career to him. I think there is a ton of people, a ton of people who owe their career to Molly and to Countdown. He nurtured Australian talent. His idea with Countdown and the producer's idea with Countdown was to bring Australian music up to the level of international music and I think they did that and they did that really, really well.
Speaker 2: And that speaks to what a different time it was in the industry as well, doesn't it? Because people just didn't have the access that they do today.
Speaker 1: There was no streaming.
Speaker 2: There was just local radio stations and three TV channels and that was kind of it.
Speaker 1: Yeah.
Speaker 2: Having someone like Molly Meldrum introduce new music and new artists, that was.
Speaker 1: Make or break. Influential. Influential. And it was appointment viewing. If you missed an episode of Countdown at six o'clock on a Sunday, I know for me personally, I would beat myself up the next day because everybody at school would be talking about it Monday in the playground. And it got to the point where ABC actually started repeating last Sunday's episode on the Saturday. So if you missed it, you could watch it again. But everybody watch Countdown. Its influence, it's hard to quantify really in words how influential it was.
Speaker 2: Tell me a little more about its influence on you and your career.
Speaker 1: Well, as I said earlier, you know, he made the art, Molly made the art of interviewing pop stars look like the best job in the world and I wanted to be a music journalist solely because of Molly. And as I said, you know, I ended up on Recovery co-presenting a three-hour live music show. I was doing a lot of press around Recovery at the time and Molly, I would always name drop Molly because he was such an influence on me and Molly actually found out about it and I ended up going to his house in Richmond in the 90s and sitting with him. And I did say to him, look, it's because of you. I'm, I'm pursuing this music journalism, you know, radio announcer, TV presenter role. He said, yep, I've been reading all the press that you've, all the lovely things you've been saying about me. Thank you so much. And, you know, that started a friendship that, you know, I ended up living in Richmond in the kind of mid 2000s and he became a neighbor and, I used to even take pasta to his house sometimes if I had leftovers. And his nickname for me was Career Girl, which was a name I didn't really love, but he was right in a sense.
Speaker 2: And I mean, everyone who's spent any time with Molly has stories about what he was like.
Speaker 1: Are there any that you would like to share?
Speaker 4: Molly, unbeknownst to a lot of people, Molly loved catalogue shopping. He'd get these big catalogues, which were the size of phone books, and he'd have them kind of splayed around his lounge room.
Speaker 1: And he admitted to me that he loved buying crap. In his words, he said, I love buying crap, Jane. I love buying crap. So he would go through, pour through all these catalogs and circle what he wanted to buy, which was really crap, and then make the phone call to order it. And so he'd always have these deliveries of crap coming to his door. But the most funniest thing he told me was, When he rang up one of these catalogue companies to order some stuff, he got a lady on the phone. The poor lady was so confused about his name. So she's saying, right, so Molly is your wife? Molly Meldrum is your wife? And he's going, no, I'm Molly Meldrum. And he said it was an absolute catastrophe, but the way he told the story was very, very funny. That's great. And what about his legacy? How do you think he's going to be remembered? Oh, look, there is nobody like Molly Meldrum, and he did more for Australian music than any other person in this country.
Speaker 3: So....
Speaker 1: How will he be remembered? I think A, as everybody's friend, like everybody in the music industry knew and loved Molly. You know, some people ran their tether with him. You know, he wasn't perfect. In fact, he named one of his biography, well, Nobody's Perfect. You know, he had his little foibles and people who love and accept Molly knew that. But You know, I think there was such a warmth to Molly because he had a good heart inherently and he always wanted to do right by artists. And I know that most of the music industry who came into Molly's path, you know, are feeling the effects of Molly's death today. His legacy is he broke Australian music in a way and championed Australian music in a way that I don't think we'll ever see ever again. And I know I am personally and professionally grateful to Molly, you know, for introducing me to a cavalcade of bands that were on national television. You know, I'm so grateful for that. Well, Dane, thank you for speaking with me. Oh, it's an absolute pleasure, Ruby. Thank you.
Speaker 2: Also in the news, the Coalition and the Greens have labelled the collapse of global climate talks a major failure by the Albanese government after talks ended without an overarching agreement. The COP31 summit collapsed after countries, including those in the European Union, rejected a draft agreement that failed to commit to moving away from fossil fuels. Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen, who co-chaired the negotiations, says the outcome is deeply disappointing... but insists progress was made on other climate commitments. And Treasurer Jim Chalmers has warned Australia's unemployment rate is expected to rise above 5% as the economy continues to slow. In a statement to Parliament, Chalmers said Treasury is forecasting weaker economic growth, higher inflation and rising unemployment. The Treasurer says the government is preparing spending cuts in next month's budget update, but neither Treasury nor the Reserve.
Speaker 1: Bank is forecasting a recession. I'm Ruby Jones. This is 7am. Thanks for listening.
